claim: Embryonic polarity of invertebrates, amphibians and fish is specified largely by maternal determinants, which fixes cell fates early in development.
source: Embryonic polarity of invertebrates, amphibians and fish is specified largely by maternal determinants, which fixes cell fates early in development.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about embryonic polarity determination in non-amniote organisms.

claim: Amniote embryos remain plastic and can form multiple individuals until gastrulation.
source: In contrast, amniote embryos remain plastic and can form multiple individuals until gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations provided later in the manuscript about twinning in amniotes.

claim: cVg1 is the earliest known factor in chick embryo polarity determination and is expressed posteriorly before gastrulation.
source: In the chick embryo, the earliest known factor is cVg1 (homologous to mammalian growth differentiation factor 1, GDF1), a transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signal expressed posteriorly before gastrulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge about cVg1 expression patterns.

claim: Pitx2 is a direct regulator of cVg1 expression.
source: We show that Pitx2 is essential for axis formation, and that it acts as a direct regulator of cVg1 expression by binding to enhancers within neighbouring genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including ChIP and reporter assays.

claim: Pitx2 binds to enhancers within neighbouring genes to regulate cVg1 expression.
source: We show that Pitx2 is essential for axis formation, and that it acts as a direct regulator of cVg1 expression by binding to enhancers within neighbouring genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experiments and enhancer reporter assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Pitx2, Vg1/GDF1 and Nodal are key actors in left–right asymmetry.
source: Pitx2, Vg1/GDF1 and Nodal are also key actors in left–right asymmetry, suggesting that the same ancient polarity determination mechanism has been co-opted to different functions during evolution.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on left-right asymmetry.

claim: The same ancient polarity determination mechanism has been co-opted to different functions during evolution.
source: Pitx2, Vg1/GDF1 and Nodal are also key actors in left–right asymmetry, suggesting that the same ancient polarity determination mechanism has been co-opted to different functions during evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation that the same genes are involved in both axis formation and left-right asymmetry.

claim: Separation of the first two blastomeres in invertebrates and anamniotes can lead to twinning.
source: Separation of the first two blastomeres can lead to twinning: the formation of genetically identical, complete individuals (Driesch, 1892).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Driesch, 1892.

claim: Separation of blastomeres after the four-cell stage in invertebrates and anamniotes does not generate twins.
source: Separation of blastomeres after the four-cell stage, however, does not generate twins; in most cases it interferes with development of even a single embryo owing to the removal of important determinants that have by then segregated to different cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mosaic development.

claim: Some species of the armadillo genus Dasypus generate quadruplets or octuplets from a single fertilisation event.
source: Some species of the armadillo genus Dasypus generate quadruplets or octuplets from a single fertilisation event, as a result of two or more sequential 'splitting' events of the embryo at a stage when it is already highly multicellular (Newman and Patterson, 1910; Loughry et al., 1998; Enders, 2002; Eakin and Behringer, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Conjoined twins occur in mammals including humans, reptiles, and birds.
source: Conjoined ('Siamese') twins occur in mammals including humans (Chai and Crary, 1971; Vanderzon et al., 1998; Kaufman, 2004) and are also seen in reptiles (Cunningham, 1937) and birds (Ulshafer and Clavert, 1979)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Most conjoined twins are thought to arise from splitting of the embryo relatively late in development.
source: most of these are thought to arise from splitting of the embryo relatively late in development (Kaufman, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaufman, 2004.

claim: Cutting a chick embryo into fragments at the blastoderm stage can lead to each fragment generating a complete embryo.
source: Perhaps the most dramatic example is seen in the chick, where cutting an embryo into fragments at the blastoderm stage (when the embryo contains as many as 20,000–50,000 cells) can lead to each fragment generating a complete embryo
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lutz, 1949 and Spratt and Haas, 1960.

claim: Up to eight embryos have been generated from a single chick blastoderm by experimental splitting.
source: up to eight embryos have been generated from a single blastoderm by experimental splitting, right up to the time of appearance of the primitive streak (Lutz, 1949; Spratt and Haas, 1960).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lutz, 1949 and Spratt and Haas, 1960.

claim: The ability of higher vertebrate embryos to retain regulative development until late stages suggests that localisation of maternally inherited determinants is not essential for specifying embryo polarity.
source: The ability of higher vertebrate embryos to retain a regulative model of development until such a late stage strongly suggests that localisation of maternally inherited determinants is not an essential component of the mechanisms specifying embryo polarity (Stern and Downs, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of regulative development, supported by a citation.

claim: Mechanisms must exist that suppress the ability to form multiple embryos in regions that do not normally initiate axis formation.
source: Moreover, since a single blastoderm can generate multiple embryos, mechanisms must exist that suppress this ability in regions of the embryo that do not normally initiate axis formation (Bertocchini and Stern, 2002; Bertocchini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that single blastoderms can generate multiple embryos, supported by citations.

claim: cVg1 is the chick orthologue of mammalian growth differentiation factor 1 (GDF1).
source: In chick embryos, the earliest symmetry breaking event known is the localised expression of cVg1, the chick orthologue of mammalian growth differentiation factor 1 (GDF1)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of gene orthology.

claim: cVg1 is a member of the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) superfamily of secreted proteins.
source: a member of the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) superfamily of secreted proteins—encoding a Nodal/Activin-type molecule that signals through Smad2/3 (Weeks and Melton, 1987; Thomsen and Melton, 1993; Kessler and Melton, 1995; Seleiro et al., 1996; Shah et al., 1997; Kessler, 2004; Birsoy et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2006; Andersson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: cVg1 encodes a Nodal/Activin-type molecule that signals through Smad2/3.
source: encoding a Nodal/Activin-type molecule that signals through Smad2/3 (Weeks and Melton, 1987; Thomsen and Melton, 1993; Kessler and Melton, 1995; Seleiro et al., 1996; Shah et al., 1997; Kessler, 2004; Birsoy et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2006; Andersson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Before primitive streak stages, cVg1 is expressed in the posterior marginal zone (PMZ).
source: Before primitive streak stages, cVg1 is expressed in the posterior marginal zone (PMZ), an extraembryonic region adjacent to where the primitive streak will form
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Misexpression of cVg1 in other parts of the marginal zone is sufficient to induce a complete axis from adjacent embryonic cells.
source: misexpression of cVg1 in other (anterior or lateral) parts of the marginal zone is sufficient to induce a complete axis from adjacent embryonic cells (Seleiro et al., 1996; Shah et al., 1997; Skromne and Stern, 2001, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanisms that position cVg1 in the PMZ are unknown.
source: The mechanisms that position cVg1 in the PMZ are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: When a blastoderm is cut in half at right angles to the future primitive streak axis, cVg1 expression spontaneously initiates in the marginal zone adjacent to the cut edge.
source: Moreover, when a blastoderm is cut in half at right angles to the future primitive streak axis, cVg1 expression spontaneously initiates in the marginal zone adjacent to the cut edge, in either the right or left side at equal frequency, foreshadowing the appearance of the primitive streak a few hours later (Bertocchini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bertocchini et al., 2004.

claim: cVg1 expression initiates in either the right or left side at equal frequency in bisected blastoderms.
source: cVg1 expression spontaneously initiates in the marginal zone adjacent to the cut edge, in either the right or left side at equal frequency, foreshadowing the appearance of the primitive streak a few hours later (Bertocchini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bertocchini et al., 2004.

claim: The mechanisms that position cVg1 are active in the blastoderm stage embryo.
source: This observation shows that the mechanisms that position cVg1 are active in the blastoderm stage embryo.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that cVg1 expression can be initiated in bisected blastoderms.

claim: A molecular screen was performed to identify upstream regulators of cVg1 using PMZ and AMZ explants from 40 embryos in triplicate.
source: We therefore performed two screens. First, we dissected the PMZ and an equivalent anterior explant (anterior marginal zone, AMZ) from 40 embryos (in triplicate) and analysed their transcriptomes using Affymetrix microarrays (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Approximately 36 out of 40 embryos were dissected correctly in each replicate of the first screen.
source: From each set of 40 embryos, approximately 36 had been dissected correctly; the explants from the remainder (3 × 4) were discarded (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the quality control results from the experimental procedure.

claim: The first screen identified 122 sequences (corresponding to 85 genes) with putative 'cVg1-like' expression.
source: Using a threshold of just 1.2-fold change and p < 0.05, this strategy identified 122 sequences (corresponding to 85 genes) with putative 'cVg1-like' expression (a cVg1-synexpression group)
evidence: This is a result from the microarray data analysis.

claim: There is highly significant correlation between the top 'Vg1-like' candidates from whole embryos and half-embryos (Spearman's rank Rho = 0.73; p = 0.00036).
source: Comparison of the top 'Vg1-like' candidates from whole embryos (PMZ vs AMZ) with their counterparts from half-embryos shows highly significant correlation (Spearman's rank Rho = 0.73; p = 0.00036).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the microarray data.

claim: cVg1 is upregulated 4.3 fold in the PMZ of whole embryos with a p value of 0.00006.
source: Confirming that the screen was performed appropriately, cVg1 (incorrectly annotated as GDF3 instead of GDF1 in the current version of the chicken genome, Galgal4) itself appears among the top genes: it is upregulated 4.3 fold, with a p value of 0.00006 (rank 11) in whole embryos
evidence: This is a result from the microarray data analysis.

claim: cVg1 is upregulated 1.71 fold in isolated anterior halves with p = 0.0062.
source: and 1.71, p = 0.0062 in the isolated anterior half (rank 21).
evidence: This is a result from the microarray data analysis.

claim: Pitx2 is the top transcription factor on the list of cVg1-like genes.
source: Among all genes, Pitx2 immediately stands out as the best candidate, being very strongly co-regulated with cVg1 and the top transcription factor on the list.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the microarray data results.

claim: In the PMZ of whole embryos Pitx2 is upregulated almost 10-fold compared to the AMZ explants.
source: In the PMZ of whole embryos Pitx2 is upregulated almost 10-fold compared to the AMZ explants (three different probes, ranking two, three and eight on the list; p = 0.0001, 0.00019 and 0.003 respectively)
evidence: This is a result from the microarray data analysis.

claim: In cut halves Pitx2 is upregulated by about 2.4 fold.
source: whereas in the cut halves it is upregulated by about 2.4 fold (three probes ranking four, six and eight on the list; p between 0.002–0.008).
evidence: This is a result from the microarray data analysis.

claim: Pitx2-MO targeted to the right edge of an isolated anterior half shifts the frequency of axis formation to the opposite side.
source: When a translation-blocking Pitx2-MO was targeted to the right edge of an isolated anterior half embryo, the frequency of axis formation shifted to the opposite side (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—source data 1A,B)
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: Pitx2-MO on the right side of isolated anterior halves generated a majority (9/10, p = 0.05) of embryos with no cVg1 expression 7 hr post-electroporation.
source: In contrast, Pitx2-MO on the right generated a majority (9/10, p = 0.05) of embryos with no expression and the remaining embryo with expression on the opposite side 7 hr post-electroporation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data1B).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: After 16 hr, embryos electroporated with Pitx2-MO on the right formed a streak on the left side in 8/10 cases and 2 had two streaks, but no embryo formed a single streak arising from the MO-transfected side (p = 0.026).
source: After 16 hr (Figure 4—source data1B) embryos electroporated with control-MO at the right edge formed a primitive streak expressing Brachyury randomly; with Pitx2-MO on the right (Figures 4B), 8/10 embryos formed a streak on the left side and 2 had two streaks (one from each corner), but no embryo formed a single streak arising from the MO-transfected side (hypergeometric exact test with 2 × 3 contingency table, p = 0.026).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Control-MO embryos transfected on the left formed a Bra-expressing streak on the right randomly, while Pitx2-MO embryos formed a streak on the right in 2/8 cases, none on the left, 1/8 on both sides and 5/8 with no streak (p = 0.003).
source: After 16 hr, control embryos transfected on the left formed a Bra-expressing streak on the right, again randomly, while Pitx2-MO embryos formed a streak on the right in 2/8 cases, none on the left, 1/8 on both sides and 5/8 with no streak (p = 0.003) (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data1B).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: In intact embryos electroporated at stage X, Pitx2-MO affected cVg1 expression after 5 hr (0/6 embryos expressing; p < 0.001).
source: With Pitx2-MO, cVg1 expression was affected after 5 hr (0/6 embryos expressing; p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Embryos started to recover from Pitx2-MO knockdown at later time points: at 12 hr, 3/12 had a normal streak, 3/12 had a displaced streak, 3/12 had two streaks, and 3/12 had no streaks (p = 0.1).
source: Embryos started to recover, however, at later time points: at 12 hr, 3/12 had a normal streak, 3/12 had a displaced streak, 3/12 had two streaks, and the remaining 3/12 had no streaks (p = 0.1—not significantly different).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: By 16 hr after Pitx2-MO electroporation, the majority of the embryos were normal (7/8; the remaining embryo had a displaced streak).
source: By 16 hr, the majority of the embryos were normal (7/8; the remaining embryo had a displaced streak) (Figure 4F; Figure 4—source data 1D).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: Pitx1 expression increased considerably after Pitx2-MO electroporation (6/6 embryos).
source: After Pitx2-MO electroporation, expression increased considerably (6/6 embryos; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from in situ hybridization experiments following morpholino knockdown.

claim: Pitx1+2-MOs caused loss of cVg1 at 5 hr in 6/6 cases (p = 0.005).
source: Pitx1+2-MOs caused loss of cVg1 at 5 hr in 6/6 cases (p = 0.005).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: By 12 hr after Pitx1+2-MO electroporation, 1/9 embryos had a normal streak, 3/9 had a displaced streak, 3/9 had two streaks and 2/9 had none (p = 0.043).
source: By 12 hr 1/9 embryos had a normal streak, 3/9 had a displaced streak, 3/9 had two streaks and 2/9 had none (p = 0.043).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: By 16 hr after Pitx1+2-MO electroporation, no recovery was observed: 4/4 embryos had double streaks, neither arising from the targeted site (p = 0.029).
source: By 16 hr no recovery was observed: 4/4 embryos had double streaks, neither arising from the targeted site (p = 0.029; Figure 4G; Figure 4—source data 1E,F).
evidence: This is a result from morpholino knockdown experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Co-electroporation of Pitx1+2-MO together with a Pitx2 expression construct led to normal axis formation: in 5/6 cases cVg1 expression was restored after 5 hr incubation and by 16 hr 12/16 embryos displayed a normal streak.
source: This effect could be rescued by supplying Pitx2 alone: co-electroporation of Pitx1+2-MO together with a Pitx2 expression construct lacking the MO target sequence led to normal axis formation: in 5/6 cases cVg1 expression was restored after 5 hr incubation and by 16 hr 12/16 embryos displayed a normal streak (Figure 4H; Figure 4—source data 1G–H).
evidence: This is a result from rescue experiments.

claim: In isolated anterior halves with Pitx1+2-MO and Pitx2 rescue, cVg1 expression was seen on the right in 4/10, on the left in 3/10, and in neither in 3/10 cases.
source: After electroporation on the right, cVg1 expression was seen on the right in 4/10, on the left in 3/10, and in neither in 3/10 cases (Figure 4J; Figure 4—source data 1K).
evidence: This is a result from rescue experiments in isolated anterior halves.

claim: After 16 hr in isolated anterior halves with Pitx1+2-MO and Pitx2 rescue, a primitive streak developed on the right in 3/8 cases, on the left in 2/8 and no streak in 3/8 cases.
source: After 16 hr a primitive streak developed on the right in 3/8 cases, on the left in 2/8 and no streak in 3/8 cases (Figure 4—source data l).
evidence: This is a result from rescue experiments in isolated anterior halves.

claim: Pitx2 is required for expression of cVg1 in the PMZ as well as for formation of the normal primitive streak.
source: In conclusion, Pitx2 is required for expression of cVg1 in the PMZ as well as for formation of the normal primitive streak.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: In isolated anterior halves, Pitx2 is required both for cVg1 expression and for the later formation of a primitive streak.
source: In isolated anterior halves, Pitx2 is required both for cVg1 expression and for the later formation of a primitive streak.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morpholino knockdown experiments in isolated anterior halves.

claim: Knockdown of Pitx2 is followed by upregulation of the related transcription factor Pitx1, which can partly compensate for the loss of Pitx2.
source: Knockdown of Pitx2 is followed by upregulation of the related transcription factor Pitx1, which can partly compensate for the loss of Pitx2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of Pitx1 upregulation after Pitx2 knockdown and the recovery phenotype.

claim: The cVg1 gene is erroneously annotated as GDF3 in the chick genome; its orthologue is human GDF1.
source: The cVg1 gene (erroneously annotated as GDF3 in the chick genome; its orthologue is human GDF1, as confirmed by synteny; see Figure 5) is located on chicken chromosome 28.
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cVg1 gene is located on chicken chromosome 28.
source: The cVg1 gene (erroneously annotated as GDF3 in the chick genome; its orthologue is human GDF1, as confirmed by synteny; see Figure 5) is located on chicken chromosome 28.
evidence: This is based on genomic location information.

claim: Conserved CTCF-binding sites are predicted about 200 kB upstream and about 100 kB downstream of cVg1/GDF3.
source: The insulator-predicting software identifies strongly conserved CTCF-binding sites about 200 kB upstream and about 100 kB downstream of cVg1/GDF3 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from computational prediction using the insulator-predicting software.

claim: The cVg1/GDF3 gene is bicistronic, with upstream exons encoding Lass1/CERS1 and the last two exons containing the cVg1 sequence.
source: The cVg1/GDF3 gene itself is bicistronic, the upstream exons encoding Lass1/CERS1 and the last two exons containing the cVg1 sequence (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2007.

claim: CERS1/LASS1, COPE, HOMER3, and UPF1 are all expressed in a similar domain of the PMZ as cVg1.
source: Strikingly, all genes examined (CERS1/LASS1, COPE, HOMER3, and UPF1) are expressed in a similar domain of the PMZ as cVg1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: DREiVe identifies six domains (E1–E6) ranging in size from 600–3000 bases, located within the introns of CERS1/LASS1 and Homer3 in chick.
source: We then applied the DREiVe tool (Discovery of Regulatory Elements in Vertebrates, the vertebrate version of EDGI) (Sosinsky et al., 2007; Khan et al., 2013), to identify de novo conserved sequence motifs around this region. This identifies six domains (designated E1–E6), ranging in size from 600–3000 bases, located within the introns of CERS1/LASS1 and of the neighbouring Homer3 in chick (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from computational prediction using DREiVe.

claim: Four of the predicted regions (E1, E3, E5, and E6) contain one or more putative binding sites for Pitx2 and/or Pitx1.
source: Analysis of these regions using Position Frequency Matrices from JASPAR and TRANSFAC databases together with the algorithms Matrix-Scan (from RSAT) and Clover predicts four of these regions (E1, E3, E5, and E6) to contain one or more putative binding sites for Pitx2 and/or the related factor Pitx1 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from computational prediction using transcription factor binding site analysis.

claim: DREiVe is able to identify homologous non-coding regions in the human genome where the syntenic region is inverted and the orthologous elements are found in a different order.
source: The power of DREiVe as a tool for discovering regulatory elements is highlighted by the observation that it is able to identify homologous non-coding regions in the human genome, where the syntenic region (on chromosome 19) is not only inverted but also the orthologous elements are found in a different order, within introns of different neighbouring genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result demonstrating the capability of the DREiVe computational tool.

claim: A monoclonal antibody against Pitx2 precipitated chromatin from the PMZ more effectively than from the AMZ for all predicted enhancers that contained consensus Pitx1/2-binding sites (especially E3, E5, and E6).
source: A monoclonal antibody against Pitx2 precipitated chromatin from the PMZ more effectively than from the AMZ for all predicted enhancers that contained consensus Pitx1/2-binding sites (especially E3, E5, and E6) but not those that do not (E2 and E4).
evidence: This is a result from ChIP experiments.

claim: Pitx2 is differentially bound to putative enhancer sites E3, E5, and E6 in the PMZ of normal embryos.
source: These findings suggest that Pitx2 is differentially bound to putative enhancer sites E3, E5, and E6 in the PMZ of normal embryos.
evidence: This is an inference from the ChIP experiment results.

claim: Enhancers E5 and E6 showed the greatest differential activity in the PMZ relative to the AMZ for H3K27ac.
source: We also tested each of the six putative enhancer regions for acetylation of Lys-27 of Histone-3 (H3K27ac), which is associated with active enhancers (Creyghton et al., 2010). Enhancers E5 and E6 showed the greatest differential activity in the PMZ relative to the AMZ.
evidence: This is a result from ChIP experiments for H3K27ac.

claim: E3, E5, and E6 are the most likely enhancers driving expression in the PMZ.
source: Together, these results suggest that E3, E5, and E6 are the most likely enhancers driving expression in the PMZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP experiment results.

claim: In whole embryos, E3 and E5 are most efficient in driving expression of the reporter in the PMZ.
source: In whole embryos, E3 and E5 are most efficient in driving expression of the reporter in the PMZ (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from reporter assay experiments.

claim: E3 and E5 also drive expression in the cVg1-expressing side in isolated anterior halves.
source: The same two enhancers also drive expression in the cVg1-expressing side in isolated anterior halves (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a result from reporter assay experiments in isolated anterior halves.

claim: Mutations in either of the Pitx-binding sites or in both binding sites of E1 still showed GFP expression without selectivity, in the middle of the embryo.
source: In whole embryos, mutations in either of the Pitx-binding sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B) or in both binding sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) of E1 still showed GFP expression without selectivity, in the middle of the embryo.
evidence: This is a result from reporter assay experiments with mutated enhancers.

claim: Mutations of any of the Pitx-binding sites in E3 or E5 completely eliminated expression in the cVg1-expressing corner of the isolated half.
source: Similar results were found in isolated anterior half-embryos: mutations of any of the Pitx-binding sites in E3 or E5 completely eliminated expression in the cVg1-expressing corner of the isolated half (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from reporter assay experiments with mutated enhancers in isolated anterior halves.

claim: cVg1 expression is regulated directly by Pitx2/Pitx1 binding to an enhancer (E5) within an intron of the HOMER3 gene.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that cVg1 expression is regulated directly by Pitx2/Pitx1 binding to an enhancer (E5) within an intron of the HOMER3 gene, adjacent to cVg1/GDF3, and to an intronic enhancer (E3) within the Lass1/CERS1 locus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP and reporter assay experiments.

claim: cVg1 expression is regulated directly by Pitx2/Pitx1 binding to an intronic enhancer (E3) within the Lass1/CERS1 locus.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that cVg1 expression is regulated directly by Pitx2/Pitx1 binding to an enhancer (E5) within an intron of the HOMER3 gene, adjacent to cVg1/GDF3, and to an intronic enhancer (E3) within the Lass1/CERS1 locus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP and reporter assay experiments.

claim: The same enhancers (E3 and E5) are involved in controlling cVg1 expression in the normal PMZ as in the portion of the lateral marginal zone where cVg1 is upregulated after isolation of a portion of embryo.
source: The same enhancers (E3 and E5) are involved in controlling cVg1 expression in the normal PMZ as in the portion of the lateral marginal zone where cVg1 is upregulated a few hours after isolation of a portion of embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reporter assay experiments in both whole embryos and isolated anterior halves.

claim: Pitx2 is the earliest gene described to date that regulates the position of the embryonic axis as well as embryonic regulation/regeneration and twinning.
source: These results implicate the transcription factor Pitx2 as the earliest gene described to date that regulates the position of the embryonic axis as well as embryonic regulation/regeneration and twinning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental results in the study.

claim: The PMZ of the chick embryo is the equivalent of the Nieuwkoop centre of amphibians.
source: The PMZ of the chick embryo is the equivalent of the Nieuwkoop centre of amphibians: it can induce a complete axis including the organiser from neighbouring cells, without making a cellular contribution to the axis (Azar and Eyal-Giladi, 1979; Khaner and Eyal-Giladi, 1989; Bachvarova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PMZ can induce a complete axis including the organiser from neighbouring cells, without making a cellular contribution to the axis.
source: it can induce a complete axis including the organiser from neighbouring cells, without making a cellular contribution to the axis (Azar and Eyal-Giladi, 1979; Khaner and Eyal-Giladi, 1989; Bachvarova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: To act, cVg1 requires canonical Wnt, which seems to be provided mainly by cWnt8C, expressed all around the marginal zone.
source: To act, cVg1 requires canonical Wnt, which seems to be provided mainly by cWnt8C, expressed all around the marginal zone (Skromne and Stern, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skromne and Stern, 2001.

claim: A target of cVg1 and Wnt is Nodal, transcribed in area pellucida cells next to the cVg1+Wnt expression domain.
source: A target of cVg1 and Wnt is Nodal, transcribed in area pellucida cells next to the cVg1+Wnt expression domain (Skromne and Stern, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skromne and Stern, 2002.

claim: The anterior end of the embryo has an early identity, defined by the expression of GATA binding protein 2 (GATA2).
source: The anterior end of the embryo also has an early identity, defined by the expression of GATA binding protein 2 (GATA2) (Sheng and Stern, 1999; Bertocchini and Stern, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Unlike cVg1, GATA2 is not a sufficient determinant of polarity and at best only acts as a bias.
source: However, unlike cVg1, GATA2 is not a sufficient determinant of polarity and at best only acts as a bias (Bertocchini and Stern, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bertocchini and Stern, 2012.

claim: In an isolated anterior half, a visible primitive streak can be detected about 12 hr after cutting.
source: In an isolated anterior half, a visible primitive streak (and expression of Brachyury and Snail2) can be detected about 12 hr after cutting.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The primitive streak appears randomly from either the left or right area pellucida adjacent to the cut edge of the marginal zone in isolated anterior halves.
source: This appears randomly from either the left or right area pellucida adjacent to the cut edge of the marginal zone (Spratt and Haas, 1960), preceded at least 6 hr earlier by expression of cVg1 in the right or left marginal zone (Bertocchini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blocking cVg1 on one side of the marginal zone of an isolated anterior half will cause the axis to arise from the opposite side.
source: Blocking cVg1 on one side of the marginal zone of an isolated anterior half will cause the axis to arise from the opposite side.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: A similar manipulation in the PMZ will cause a streak to arise from outside the MO-electroporated domain.
source: A similar manipulation in the PMZ will cause a streak to arise from outside the MO-electroporated domain (Bertocchini et al., 2004; Bertocchini and Stern, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: cVg1 expression in the marginal zone is both necessary and sufficient to initiate formation of a primitive streak.
source: Thus, cVg1 expression in the marginal zone is both necessary and sufficient to initiate formation of a primitive streak.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pitx transcription factors are characterised by possessing a Lysine residue at position 50 of the homeodomain.
source: Pitx transcription factors are characterised by possessing a Lysine residue at position 50 of the homeodomain, an unusual property shared with the vertebrate genes Goosecoid and OTX-1/2 and with the founder gene of the family, Drosophila Bicoid.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Pitx transcription factors.

claim: In Drosophila, Bicoid is a critical specifier of 'anterior' identity and essential for setting up head–tail polarity of the early embryo.
source: In Drosophila, Bicoid is a critical specifier of 'anterior' identity and essential for setting up head–tail polarity of the early embryo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Bicoid in Drosophila.

claim: The Bicoid gene does not appear to have direct orthologues in species other than schizophoran flies.
source: Although it is tempting to speculate that a Bicoid/Pitx system may have an ancient function in the specification of head–tail polarity, the Bicoid gene does not appear to have direct orthologues in species other than schizophoran flies (closely related to Drosophila), so this may be either a coincidence or convergent evolution.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Bicoid evolution.

claim: Pitx2, cVg1/GDF1, Tbx6, and Nodal are involved in specifying left–right asymmetry in different vertebrate classes.
source: The four key components that form part of this gene regulatory network initiating axis formation, Pitx2, cVg1/GDF1, Tbx6, and Nodal, are also involved a little later in development (from the late primitive streak stage) in specifying left–right asymmetry in different vertebrate classes (Levin et al., 1995; Hyatt et al., 1996; Hyatt and Yost, 1998; Logan et al., 1998; Meno et al., 1998; Piedra et al., 1998; Ryan et al., 1998; St Amand et al., 1998; Yoshioka et al., 1998; Zhu et al., 1999; Rankin et al., 2000; Wall et al., 2000; Levin, 2005; Raya and Izpisua Belmonte, 2006; Tanaka et al., 2007; Hadjantonakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Pitx2, cVg1/GDF1, Tbx6, and Nodal are the main conserved components of the left–right pathway among different vertebrates.
source: Indeed, these are the main conserved components of the left–right pathway among different vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: The left–right pathway may have evolved by co-opting a more ancient mechanism for initiating formation of the gastrular axis.
source: These observations raise the possibility that the left–right pathway may have evolved by co-opting a more ancient mechanism for initiating formation of the gastrular axis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation that the same genes are involved in both processes.

claim: A Nodal/Pitx2 loop is involved in specifying both left–right asymmetry and mesendoderm formation (oral-aboral polarity) in the sea urchin.
source: This is supported by the finding that a Nodal/Pitx2 loop is involved in specifying both left–right asymmetry and mesendoderm formation (oral-aboral polarity) in the sea urchin, a non-vertebrate deuterostome (Duboc et al., 2004; Hibino et al., 2006; Warner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on sea urchin development.

claim: Pitx2, Vg1, Nodal, and Tbx6 are involved in early mesendoderm development in anamniotes.
source: Pitx2, Vg1, Nodal, and Tbx6 are also involved in early mesendoderm development in anamniotes, although Vg1 is maternal (Thomsen and Melton, 1993; Kessler and Melton, 1995; Faucourt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the mouse, double mutants for Pitx1 and Pitx2 lead to early lethality (at pre- or peri-implantation stages) of the embryo.
source: In the mouse, double mutants for Pitx1 and Pitx2 lead to early lethality (at pre- or peri-implantation stages) of the embryo (Marcil et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcil et al., 2003.

claim: Only a single Pitx1/Pitx2 double mutant mouse embryo was ever recovered that had survived to E10–E12.
source: Only a single embryo was ever recovered that had survived to E10–E12 (Drouin, personal communication).
evidence: This is based on a personal communication.

claim: The strong conservation of the active enhancers (E3 and E5, including the Pitx-binding sites) near mouse and human GDF1 suggests that this is likely to be a conserved feature of birds and mammals.
source: Certainly, the strong conservation of the active enhancers (E3 and E5, including the Pitx-binding sites contained therein) near mouse and human GDF1 suggests that this is likely to be a conserved feature of birds and mammals
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of enhancers shown in the study.

claim: The retention of a regulative mode of development at late stages by amniote embryos evolved through novel uses of an ancient pathway involved in both mesendoderm development and left–right asymmetry.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the retention of a regulative mode of development at late stages by amniote embryos (that allows the formation of the types of monozygotic twins that arise relatively late in development, including Siamese twins) evolved through novel uses of an ancient pathway, involved in both mesendoderm development and left–right asymmetry, but in slightly different ways.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Pitx2 can be detected in isolated anterior halves 3 hr after cutting.
source: With this strategy we detected cVg1 expression 4–5 hr after cutting (Figure 3L–P), 1–2 hr earlier than in previous reports (Bertocchini et al., 2004), while Pitx2 appeared even earlier, just 3 hr after embryo bisection (Figure 3G–K).
evidence: This is a result from in situ hybridization experiments with extended development time.

claim: cVg1 can be detected in isolated anterior halves 4–5 hr after cutting, 1–2 hr earlier than in previous reports.
source: With this strategy we detected cVg1 expression 4–5 hr after cutting (Figure 3L–P), 1–2 hr earlier than in previous reports (Bertocchini et al., 2004)
evidence: This is a result from in situ hybridization experiments with extended development time.

claim: Pitx2 is expressed in the PMZ already at the time of laying (stage X).
source: We detected Pitx2 in the PMZ by the time of laying, stage X (Figure 3A), where it remains until early streak stages (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is a result from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Pitx2 is expressed before cVg1 in both whole embryos and isolated anterior halves.
source: Taken together, these results implicate Pitx2 as a good candidate for an upstream regulator of cVg1 expression: it is a transcription factor, it is expressed in the same domain as cVg1 in whole embryos and in bisected embryo marginal zone, and it is expressed before cVg1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal expression analysis.

claim: Pitx2 is expressed in the same domain as cVg1 in whole embryos and in bisected embryo marginal zone.
source: Taken together, these results implicate Pitx2 as a good candidate for an upstream regulator of cVg1 expression: it is a transcription factor, it is expressed in the same domain as cVg1 in whole embryos and in bisected embryo marginal zone, and it is expressed before cVg1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression pattern analysis.

claim: The Pitx2/cVg1(GDF1)/Nodal pathway is a possible candidate to explain the obligate quadruplets of armadillos.
source: Our studies allow us to predict the Pitx2/cVg1(GDF1)/Nodal pathway as a possible candidate to explain the obligate quadruplets of armadillos (Newman and Patterson, 1910; Loughry et al., 1998; Enders, 2002; Eakin and Behringer, 2004) and/or the high incidence of monozygotic and conjoined twins in certain human populations (Cox, 1963; Hamamy et al., 2004; Forsberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the findings of the study.

claim: The Pitx2/cVg1(GDF1)/Nodal pathway is a possible candidate to explain the high incidence of monozygotic and conjoined twins in certain human populations.
source: Our studies allow us to predict the Pitx2/cVg1(GDF1)/Nodal pathway as a possible candidate to explain the obligate quadruplets of armadillos (Newman and Patterson, 1910; Loughry et al., 1998; Enders, 2002; Eakin and Behringer, 2004) and/or the high incidence of monozygotic and conjoined twins in certain human populations (Cox, 1963; Hamamy et al., 2004; Forsberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the findings of the study.

claim: cVg1 is first detected at around stage XI in normal embryos.
source: In normal embryos cVg1 is first detected at around stage XI (Bertocchini and Stern, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ChIP experiments suggest that Pitx2 binding to an additional intronic enhancer in HOMER3 (E6) may also be functional in the PMZ.
source: The ChIP experiments suggest that Pitx2 binding to an additional intronic enhancer in HOMER3 (E6) may also be functional in the PMZ, although this was not seen when a reporter construct containing this element was electroporated into the PMZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the ChIP results, noting a discrepancy with the reporter assay results.
